content: Endometrial ablation is a medical procedure designed to remove or destroy the endometrial lining of a woman’s uterus. This procedure is primarily used for women who experience excessive or prolonged menstrual bleeding and either cannot or do not wish to undergo a hysterectomy. It is typically performed on an outpatient basis. However, it is contraindicated in patients who may wish to conceive in the future. There are several techniques available for performing endometrial ablation. One method involves the use of the NovaSure system, where a mesh is inserted into the uterine cavity. Electrical energy is applied to the mesh, which thermally damages and destroys the adjacent endometrial tissue. Another approach involves the insertion of a balloon filled with heated fluid, which destroys the uterine lining. Older methods utilize hysteroscopy, where instruments are inserted into the uterus under direct visualization to destroy the lining using either a laser or electrical current delivered through a small loop. Another option involves the use of a radiofrequency rod that emits energy to ablate the uterine lining. The HTA (Hydrothermal Ablation) system is another alternative, where a hysteroscope—a small telescope-like device—is inserted into the uterus through the cervix to allow the physician to visualize the treatment area. Heated saline is then circulated to destroy the uterine lining. The procedure can be performed under local anesthesia, or if necessary, under general or spinal anesthesia. Recovery time varies, ranging from one day to up to two weeks. Following the procedure, the endometrial tissue heals through scarring, which significantly reduces or eliminates the possibility of future uterine bleeding. While many patients develop amenorrhea (the absence of menstrual periods), hormonal function remains unaffected. It is important to note that pregnancy is still possible after undergoing endometrial ablation, so some form of birth control must be used post-procedure. Regarding effectiveness, approximately 90% of women who undergo endometrial ablation experience a reduction in menstrual bleeding. Of these, around 45% will stop having periods entirely. However, about 22% of patients may require a second procedure or a hysterectomy at some point following the initial treatment.
